question: What does giving a drug via the intracardiac route mean?

options.A: Delivering drugs directly into the spinal canal
options.B: Injecting medication directly into the heart muscle or chambers
options.C: Pushing medication through a tube placed in the stomach
options.D: Infusing fluids through a large vein in the neck

explanation: You've got this! This rare route involves putting a needle right through the chest wall into the heart tissue to deliver emergency drugs fast. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h1)

question: Why is giving injections straight into the heart a last resort in today's hospitals?

options.A: It requires special oral preparation before injection
options.B: It takes too long for the medication to reach the brain
options.C: It can only be performed by a pharmacist in a laboratory
options.D: It carries severe risks of heart damage and safer routes usually work

explanation: Poking the heart muscle can cause serious bleeding and injury. That's why nurses and doctors always try IV or bone (intraosseous) lines first! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h1)

question: Where is the classic landmark for placing an intracardiac injection on the chest?

options.A: Second intercostal space on the right mid-clavicular line
options.B: Third intercostal space directly over the sternum
options.C: Fourth intercostal space just to the left of the sternum
options.D: Fifth intercostal space at the mid-axillary line

explanation: Spotting the right anatomical landmarks is a key nursing skill! This specific spot lets a needle reach the left ventricle while keeping surrounding chest structures safe. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h2)

question: If an intracardiac needle is placed too far to the side (laterally), which major organ might accidentally get punctured?
explanation: Great thinking! Because the lungs sit right next to the heart, pushing a needle too far sideways risks puncturing lung tissue and causing a collapse. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h2)

question: In what kind of situation would an intracardiac injection most likely be considered?

options.A: Before taking a patient for a scheduled X-ray scan
options.B: When treating mild high blood pressure in the clinic
options.C: During routine morning medication rounds on a stable ward
options.D: During severe cardiac arrest when standard IV access fails

explanation: Spot on! This high-risk technique is saved strictly for dire emergency resuscitation when no other way to give medicine is available. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h3)

question: Why does a crashing patient make standard IV drug delivery so difficult?

options.A: The skin becomes too thick for any needle to pierce
options.B: The blood begins to flow backward toward the feet
options.C: Emergency drugs are blocked by the skin's natural oil barrier
options.D: Peripheral veins flatten and collapse, making them hard to cannulate

explanation: When blood pressure drops severely, peripheral veins empty out and flatten. This makes slipping an IV cannula in super tough during an emergency! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h3)

question: What is the main job of epinephrine when used during a cardiac arrest?

options.A: Stimulates heart rate and contraction force
options.B: Lowers blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels
options.C: Relaxes the airway to help the patient breathe
options.D: Thins the blood to prevent dangerous clots

explanation: You've got this! Epinephrine acts as a powerful jump-start, waking up a stopped heart and pushing blood to vital organs. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h4)

question: Which of these medications would you NOT give directly into the heart muscle for routine pain relief?
explanation: Morphine is a pain reliever (analgesic), not a cardiac arrest drug. It is never poked straight into the heart muscle! [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h4)

question: As a nurse, what is your primary role during an emergency intracardiac injection?

options.A: Performing the needle insertion into the chest wall
options.B: Preparing equipment and monitoring the cardiac rhythm
options.C: Prescribing the correct dosage of emergency drugs
options.D: Documenting the discharge summary for the patient

explanation: Teamwork is key in emergencies! You support the doctor by getting gear ready, timing events, and watching the monitor to see how the patient reacts. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h5)

question: Why must chest compressions pause briefly when someone is giving an intracardiac injection?

options.A: To ensure the intravenous line stays securely in place
options.B: To prevent the needle from moving and tearing the heart muscle
options.C: To keep the patient from waking up during the procedure
options.D: To allow the nurse time to chart the medication administration

explanation: Safety first! CPR makes the chest bounce around, which would cause a needle inside the heart to rip the muscle tissue. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h5)

question: What is a major, life-threatening danger of an intracardiac injection?

options.A: Severe chronic kidney failure within two hours
options.B: Cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardial sac
options.C: Total loss of vision in both eyes
options.D: Permanent yellow discoloration of the skin

explanation: Spot on. If blood leaks from the needle hole into the tight sac around the heart, it squeezes the heart so hard it can't beat anymore. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h6)

question: Why is the intracardiac injection route hardly ever used in modern hospitals anymore?

options.A: Patients refusing to allow needles near their chests
options.B: New laws making emergency heart surgery illegal
options.C: The high cost of manufacturing long needles
options.D: The availability of safer and easier intraosseous and IV routes

explanation: Medical tech has advanced! Today's intraosseous drills and central lines deliver drugs super fast without putting a giant needle directly through the heart. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h6)

question: What should a nurse watch closest right after a patient gets an intracardiac injection?

options.A: Urine output using a bedside commode
options.D: Range of motion in the upper arms

explanation: You've got this! Because the heart muscle was just punctured, tracking heart rhythm and blood pressure helps catch dangerous complications right away. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h7)

question: A patient has muffled heart sounds and a sudden blood pressure crash after an intracardiac injection. What is happening?
explanation: Spot on! Blood pooling inside the sac around the heart dampens the heart sounds and stops the heart from filling with blood, crashing the blood pressure. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T14#GNS125_U3_T14_h7)
